name: Amira Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Amira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions or parties. What you say here stays confidential. Could you start by describing a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a two-boom jumbo drill underground at the nickel mine, on the 900-metre level, and I lead the drilling crew on day shift. We go down in the cage at six, I check the face, mark up the holes, and we drill a round for the blasters before lunch. I love the moment the drill bites clean and you can feel the rock is good. What wears me out is the heat down there and the old ventilation that the company keeps saying it'll fix.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Luis drives a school bus, so between us we earn just about enough. We've got two girls, eight and eleven, and a mortgage on a semi-detached place near the rail line. This mine's an older one and pays less than the big ones up north, but it's twenty minutes from home and there's nothing else near us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's a relief, now can we get the ventilation fixed. At work people would joke that the AI couldn't even write the canteen menu properly. I might share a funny article in the union group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be glad. I use the chatbot now and then to tidy up my handover notes, so a bit of time saved is fine by me. Our drilling's already half guided by the computer on the jumbo, and that's helped, not hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am. I'd keep pushing at the safety committee for the ventilation money, and maybe try to get the girls' braces paid off by summer. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit flat, maybe, because everyone made such a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the computer on the jumbo has helped. How so?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It shows me where each hole should go on a screen, so we don't overdrill and waste explosive. When it came in five years ago I didn't trust it, then after a month I saw the rounds were cleaner. That's how I am with most things, show me first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the money, which is a worry in every picture. We're always one car repair from the credit card. AI or no AI, that's my real life.

S0.say: I'd say it's a relief and then ask whether the company can finally fix the ventilation. At work people would joke about it, and I might share a funny article in the union group chat.
S0.think: Privately I'd be glad, because I use the chatbot now and then for handover notes and the guidance screen on the jumbo has helped. A small amount of time saved suits me.
S0.do: Carries on as before and keeps pushing the safety committee for ventilation money. Tries to pay off the girls' braces by summer.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat after all the fuss.
S0.quote: We're always one car repair from the credit card.
S0.fieldNote: Amira is at ease with modest tech because she has seen it work on her own drill. Her real worry is money, not machines, and it surfaces even in the calmest picture. She describes herself as needing proof before she trusts something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the union and the government need to get ahead of it, with proper retraining paid for by the companies making the savings. I'd say it calmly, though. I'm not the type to shout at meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think the jumbos go tele-remote, run from a room on the surface, and they'll need fewer of us. I've got a decent chance at one of those seats because I already know the guidance system. But I'd feel awful about the ones who don't get one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my name down for any tele-remote training the minute it's posted, and ask the supervisor straight out what the plan is. We'd stop the takeaway on Fridays and try to build a month's savings, which we've never had. I'd also go to the union's meeting on the new contract, because I want a say in who gets kept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can see a way through for me, but it's narrow, and the money means I can't afford to get it wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you feel awful about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ricky on my crew, he's brilliant with the drill and terrible with anything written down. He'd panic at a screen with six windows. I'd want the union to fight for a job for people like him, maybe in maintenance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Luis's job be affected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the other thing. If self-driving buses come in at the same time, we're both in trouble in the same year. I try not to think about that one too hard.

S1.say: I'd say the union and the government need to get ahead of it, with retraining paid for by the companies making the savings. I'd say it calmly at meetings rather than shouting.
S1.think: I really think the drills go tele-remote and fewer of us are needed. I have a decent chance at a control seat because I know the guidance system, but I'd feel terrible for crew who don't.
S1.do: Signs up for tele-remote training as soon as it's posted and asks her supervisor for the plan. Cuts the Friday takeaway to build a first month of savings and attends the union's contract meeting.
S1.feel: Anxious: she sees a narrow way through, but can't afford a mistake.
S1.quote: If self-driving buses come in at the same time, we're both in trouble in the same year.
S1.fieldNote: Amira sees a realistic path for herself in remote operation, but the household risk doubles because her husband drives a bus. She thinks about her crew as much as herself. Her approach is careful and collective rather than angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for any decent society, and the government has to slow the companies down or catch the people who fall. Income support, a pause on layoffs, something. I'd post that, and I don't usually post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think two years means even the tele-remote seats go, because the AI can run the drill without me watching it. I'd have maybe a year of work left. With what we've got saved, that's the house gone if Luis's job goes too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to the bank in the first month about what happens if we miss payments, and sell the second car. I'd ask the union to push for a guaranteed payout for anyone over ten years' service. And I'd start using the AI properly to look for anything, anywhere, that still needs a person, even if it's further away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Like being in the cage when it stops between levels and the lights flicker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move, if it came to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If there was work and we had to, yes, though the girls would hate me. My mum's three hours away and has a spare room. It's a terrible plan but it's a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the girls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it's not because their mum wasn't good at her job. My eleven-year-old notices everything, so I'd have to tell her the truth before she worked it out. And I'd tell them we stick together, because that's all we'd have.

S2.say: I'd say this is too fast for any decent society and the government must slow the companies down or catch those who fall. I'd post about income support and a pause on layoffs, which I rarely do.
S2.think: I think even the tele-remote seats would go within two years and I'd have about a year of work left. With our savings, we'd lose the house if Luis's job went too.
S2.do: Talks to the bank in the first month about missed payments and sells the second car. Pushes the union for a guaranteed payout for long-serving staff, and uses AI to search widely for work, considering a move to her mother's.
S2.feel: Frightened, like the cage stopping between levels with the lights flickering.
S2.quote: It's a terrible plan but it's a plan.
S2.fieldNote: Two years strips away the tele-remote route Amira was counting on. She turns practical fast: the bank, the second car, her mother's spare room. Her worry for her daughters' view of her was the most emotional moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them for real retraining and a proper safety net, not just speeches. I'd want the mine to publish its automation plan so families can plan too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I get a few good years in the tele-remote room, then it's over around the same time as everyone else. But three years of steady pay means we could have something saved for once. That matters more than people think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get onto the tele-remote course in year one and use the chatbot to help me study the theory, which I've done before for my ticket. We'd put away every bit of overtime, maybe two hundred a month. And I'd start a night course in something near the mine but not in it, like electrical maintenance or ventilation systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy. I do better when I've got a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ventilation systems. Is that a serious idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half serious. I've spent fifteen years complaining about the fans, I might as well learn how they work. And somebody has to fix the robots' air too, or do they not need it? I genuinely don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday to the lake, which we'd only just booked. Then the girls' dance class, which breaks my heart a bit. Luis would give up his football club fees before I asked him.

S3.say: I'd say we have five years and should use them for real retraining and a safety net, not speeches. I'd want the mine to publish its automation plan so families can plan.
S3.think: I think I'd get a few good years in the tele-remote room before the end comes for everyone. Three steady years could finally give us some savings, which matters a lot.
S3.do: Takes the tele-remote course in the first year, using the chatbot to study. Saves around two hundred a month of overtime and starts a night course in electrical or ventilation maintenance, cutting the lake holiday and dance classes.
S3.feel: Anxious but busy, steadied by having a list.
S3.quote: I've spent fifteen years complaining about the fans, I might as well learn how they work.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Amira from frightened to organised. She treats the time mainly as a chance to build savings and a second skill. She openly admitted she didn't know whether robots would even need ventilation, which was refreshingly honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this right, so let's plan it like a mine closure: on paper, with dates, and with money set aside. I'd say that in the union chat and at the school gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think ten years is the difference between a disaster and a hard change. I'd be fifty-three, the girls would be finishing school, and with luck the mortgage would be smaller. I'm not calm about it, but I'm not losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the tele-remote training, then over a few years a proper electrical certificate at night. We'd build up three months' savings slowly. I'd also make sure the girls know mining isn't a sure thing, so they choose their subjects with their eyes open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. It's like knowing the mine has ten years of ore left. You don't panic, you plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make ten years feel worse than it sounds?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company wastes it. If they say nothing for eight years and then drop it on us anyway. That's what happened when they shut the old shaft, everyone knew and nobody said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want your daughters near the mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Near it, maybe, but not under it. My eldest likes science, so maybe she ends up designing the things that replaced me. I'd find that funny, honestly.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to do it right, planned like a mine closure with dates and money set aside. I'd say it in the union chat and at the school gate.
S4.think: I think ten years is the difference between a disaster and a hard change. I'd be fifty-three with the girls finishing school and a smaller mortgage, so I'm uneasy but not losing sleep.
S4.do: Takes the tele-remote training, then an electrical certificate at night over several years. Builds three months of savings slowly and talks with her daughters about choosing school subjects beyond mining.
S4.feel: Uneasy but steady, the way miners feel about a known end to the ore.
S4.quote: Near it, maybe, but not under it.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Amira's mood settles because her life stage lines up well: kids nearly grown, mortgage shrinking. Her main fear is the company keeping quiet until the last minute, based on what happened when the old shaft closed. She found real humour in the idea of her daughter designing the machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Luis and I could both lose our jobs in the same year with nothing saved. What would help is a law that makes the company give a long notice and pay for retraining, and some kind of income support while you study, so you're not choosing between the course and the mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the women. There aren't many of us underground, and it took me years to be taken seriously on the drill. I'd hate for the new jobs to go straight back to the men just because they were in the room first.

headlineQuote: I'd hate for the new jobs to go straight back to the men just because they were in the room first.
portrait: Amira Torres is a 43-year-old jumbo drill crew lead at an older nickel mine, married to a school bus driver, with two daughters, a mortgage and almost no savings. She trusts technology once she has seen it work, and already relies on a drill guidance screen and occasional chatbot help. She stays calm if AI stalls, turns anxious and organised with steady change, and becomes frightened only when two years leaves no time to build a cushion. Throughout she thinks of her crew and her daughters, wants companies to pay for the change, and worries the new jobs will go back to men.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she and her husband could both lose their jobs in the same year with nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: A law requiring long notice and company-paid retraining, plus income support during study so she doesn't have to choose between the course and the mortgage.
